title: Marsyas. Pelops
titleEn: Marsyas Flayed; Pelops and the Ivory Shoulder — Metamorphoses VI.382–411
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Two short episodes stand under one heading here. The crowd's talk moves from Lycia to the satyr Marsyas, beaten at the pipe by Latona's son and flayed alive for it; the tears of everyone who mourned him soak into the ground and rise again as the clearest river in Phrygia. Then the talk comes back to the present and to Amphion, destroyed with his line, and to a mother whom everyone now blames — for whom one man, Pelops, weeps, pulling his clothes off his chest to show the ivory shoulder the gods gave him.
advisory: The flaying of Marsyas is described at length and in anatomical detail — the skin drawn off, the exposed sinews, veins and organs — and Lectorium presents the passage unaltered.

sentences.t:
Sic ubi nescio quis Lycia de gente virorum
rettulit exitium, satyri reminiscitur alter,
quem Tritoniaca Latous harundine victum
adfecit poena.
sentences.l: When someone or other had thus reported the destruction of the men of the Lycian people, another calls to mind the satyr — beaten with the Tritonian reed — whom Latona's son visited with punishment.
sentences.i: When one of them had told the fate of the Lycian countrymen in this way, someone else remembered the satyr whom Latona's son beat at the Tritonian pipe and then punished.
sentences.n: 'nescio quis' — literally 'I don't know who' — is a fixed idiom meaning 'someone or other'; this frame keeps its speakers anonymous throughout. 'alter' is 'the second of two', picking up from the 'unus' who told the Lycian story. 'reminiscitur' takes a genitive, 'satyri', as verbs of remembering do. 'Latous' means 'the son of Leto', i.e. Apollo, named by the mother who was the subject of the tale just ended — the join between the two stories is made through her. 'Tritoniaca harundine' is the reed-pipe of Tritonia, a title of Pallas, who made it and threw it away; Marsyas found it, and it is the instrument he lost with. 'victum' agrees with 'quem', the satyr, and not with 'Latous', which stands next to it: it is Marsyas who was beaten, and the word order is the trap.

sentences.l: 'Why do you strip me from myself?' he says.
sentences.n: The cry is one grammatical move made unbearable. 'detraho' is the ordinary verb for pulling a garment or a hide off something, and it takes an accusative of the thing removed and a dative of what it is removed from. Here the two are the same person: 'me' is being pulled off 'mihi'. The skin is him, and he is watching it taken away from him. 'inquit' is the historic present.

sentences.t: “a piget a non est” clamabat “tibia tanti.”
sentences.l: 'ah, it galls me, ah, the pipe is not worth so much,' he kept crying.
sentences.i: 'Ah, I regret it, ah — the pipe was not worth this,' he kept shouting.
sentences.n: 'a' is the interjection 'ah', printed bare in this edition. 'piget' is an impersonal verb — it galls, it disgusts, it causes remorse — with no subject at all, and it takes the person as its object; English has to attach the feeling to somebody, here as 'it galls me'. It is not the verb of an apology: what he says is that the thing revolts him. 'tanti' is a genitive of value, 'of so much worth': the pipe is not worth what it is costing him. 'clamabat' is imperfect, the shouting going on and on, and it is dropped into the middle of his own sentence so that the cry breaks over it.

sentences.t:
Clamanti cutis est summos direpta per artus,
nec quicquam nisi vulnus erat;
sentences.l: From him as he cried the skin was torn away over the surface of his limbs, and there was nothing except a wound;
sentences.i: As he cried out, his skin was torn off him over the whole surface of his limbs, and there was nothing there any more but a wound;
sentences.n: 'Clamanti' is a dative of disadvantage on a present participle — 'from him crying out'. It is the first word of the sentence, so the cry of the previous line is still going while this happens. 'summos … per artus' is 'over the tops of the limbs', the outermost surface, everywhere at once. The second clause has no subject noun of its own: what remains is not a man with a wound but simply the wound.

sentences.t:
cruor undique manat,
detectique patent nervi,
sentences.l: gore runs from everywhere, and the sinews, uncovered, lie open,
sentences.n: 'cruor' is spilled blood, blood outside the body, as against 'sanguis', the blood that belongs inside it — the choice of word is exact. 'manat' is a historic present, and the description holds that present through 'patent' and 'micant': it is happening in front of you rather than being reported, until 'posses' two lines on turns and hands the looking to you. 'detecti' is a perfect passive participle from the same 'tego' that gives 'cover' and 'roof' — literally 'un-roofed'.

sentences.t:
trepidaeque sine ulla
pelle micant venae;
sentences.l: and the veins, in a panic, flash with no skin at all over them;
sentences.n: 'trepidae' is a word for frightened people — agitated, in a panic — given here to the veins, so that the parts of the body carry the terror the man can no longer express. 'micant' is the verb for a darting or flashing movement: what would be an invisible pulse under skin is now motion you can watch. 'sine ulla … pelle' is split around the verb, the phrase itself stripped apart.

sentences.t:
salientia viscera posses
et perlucentes numerare in pectore fibras.
sentences.l: you could count the leaping innards and, in his chest, the fibres showing through.
sentences.n: 'posses' is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite 'you' — Latin's way of saying 'one could' — and it pulls the reader right up to the body to look. 'fibrae' are the lobes of the internal organs, the parts an inspector reads after a sacrifice; the vocabulary here belongs to the altar, which is what the satyr has been turned into. 'perlucentes' is 'shining through', the organs visible because nothing covers them.

sentences.t:
Illum ruricolae, silvarum numina, fauni
et satyri fratres et tunc quoque carus Olympus
et nymphae flerunt, et quisquis montibus illis
lanigerosque greges armentaque bucera pavit.
sentences.l: Him the country-dwelling fauns, divinities of the woods, and his brother satyrs, and Olympus, dear to him even then, and the nymphs wept for, and whoever pastured wool-bearing flocks and ox-horned herds on those mountains.
sentences.i: The fauns who live in the fields, gods of the woods, wept for him — and his brother satyrs, and Olympus, still dear to him even then, and the nymphs, and every man who grazed woolly flocks and horned cattle on those hills.
sentences.n: 'Illum' is the object, held at the head of the sentence while five subjects pile up behind it, and the verb 'flerunt' (= 'fleverunt', a syncopated perfect) does not arrive until the third line. The delay is the list. 'fratres' is in apposition — the satyrs are his own kind. 'lanigeros' and 'bucera' are compound adjectives, 'wool-bearing' and 'ox-horned', the second a Greek formation; such compounds raise ordinary sheep and cattle to the pitch of the rest. 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'even, also'. 'carus' has no dative expressed — dear to whom is left open, and the natural supply is Marsyas, though the phrase can also simply mean 'still dear even then', when everything else about him had been taken away; both layers make the supply and this is where it is visible.

sentences.t:
Fertilis inmaduit madefactaque terra caducas
concepit lacrimas ac venis perbibit imis;
sentences.l: The fertile earth grew wet and, once soaked, took in the falling tears and drank them down in its deepest veins;
sentences.n: 'inmaduit' keeps this edition's 'inm-' spelling where later texts print 'imm-'. 'madefacta' repeats the same root at once — wet, then made wet — and the repetition is the sound of the ground taking the water up. 'venis … imis' gives the earth veins, the very word just used of the flayed body: the landscape takes over the anatomy. 'caducas' is 'falling, apt to fall'.

sentences.t: quas ubi fecit aquam, vacuas emisit in auras.
sentences.l: and when it had made them water, it sent them out into the empty air.
sentences.n: 'quas' is a connecting relative opening the sentence — 'and these', the tears — which is one of the commonest joins in Latin; English simply uses a pronoun. 'fecit' here takes two accusatives, 'made them water'. 'vacuas … in auras' is 'out into the open air', with 'auras' plural where English wants a singular.

sentences.t:
Inde petens rapidum ripis declivibus aequor
Marsya nomen habet, Phrygiae liquidissimus amnis.
sentences.l: Thence, making for the swift sea between sloping banks, it has the name Marsyas, the clearest river of Phrygia.
sentences.i: From there it makes for the running sea between sloping banks, and it bears the name Marsyas — the clearest river in Phrygia.
sentences.n: The point of the episode: the tears become a stream and the stream keeps the man's name. 'Marsya' is the Greek nominative of the name, standing where a reader might expect an accusative after 'habet': the name is in apposition to the river that carries it, alongside 'liquidissimus amnis', so the river simply is Marsyas and the man's name is now a thing on the map. 'ripis declivibus' is an ablative of route, the banks that carry it down. 'liquidissimus' is a superlative — 'clearest' — and it is where the whole story lands: what came out of that ruined body is the purest water in the country. Magnus prints 'rapidum' with 'aequor', the sea; some editions print 'rapidus', which makes the river itself swift instead.

sentences.t:
Talibus extemplo redit ad praesentia dictis
vulgus et exstinctum cum stirpe Amphiona luget.
sentences.l: With such words the crowd at once comes back to present things, and mourns Amphion, snuffed out together with his stock.
sentences.i: With talk like that the crowd comes straight back to the present, and mourns Amphion, wiped out along with his line.
sentences.n: The frame closes: the inset stories are done and the poem picks up the scene it left. 'Talibus … dictis' is an ablative of means bracketing the whole line. 'Amphiona' is a Greek accusative of the name — Greek nouns keep Greek endings in Latin verse. 'stirps' is the root or stock of a plant, used of a family line, so 'cum stirpe' is 'root and branch'. 'exstinctum' keeps this edition's 'exst-' spelling.

sentences.i: It is the mother they hold it against.
sentences.n: 'in invidia esse' is an idiom, and it does not mean 'to be in envy': it means to be the object of resentment, the person people blame. Four words, and the crowd's sympathy has changed sides. She is not named anywhere in this stretch of the frame, which is part of the effect — she has become a position rather than a person.

sentences.t:
Hanc tunc quoque dicitur unus
flesse Pelops, umeroque, suas a pectore postquam
deduxit vestes ebur ostendisse sinistro.
sentences.l: Even then one man, Pelops, is said to have wept for her, and, after he drew his clothes down from his chest, to have shown the ivory on his left shoulder.
sentences.i: Even then, they say, one man wept for her — Pelops — and after pulling his clothes down off his chest he showed the ivory on his left shoulder.
sentences.n: 'dicitur' with infinitives again: 'is said to have wept … to have shown', the standard way of reporting legend without vouching for it. 'flesse' is syncopated 'flevisse'. 'tunc quoque' is 'even then' — when everyone else has turned against her. 'umero … sinistro' is split across two lines with the whole 'postquam' clause between, so the shoulder is named last and 'ebur', ivory, sits bare in the middle of the line as the reveal.

sentences.l: This shoulder was of one colour with the right at the time of his being born, and of flesh: they say that the gods soon joined together the limbs cut apart by his father's hands;
sentences.i: At the time he was born this shoulder matched the right one in colour, and was flesh: soon afterwards, they say, the gods put back together the limbs his father's hands had cut up;
sentences.n: 'concolor … dextro' — 'the same colour as the right' — takes a dative. 'nascendi tempore' uses a gerund in the genitive, 'at the time of being born'. 'ferunt' with accusative and infinitive is another 'they say', keeping the horror at one remove. 'manibus … paternis' with 'caesa membra': the father is Tantalus, who cut up his son and served him to the gods at table. The poem gives that in half a line and does not stop for it.

sentences.t:
aliisque repertis,
qui locus est iuguli medius summique lacerti,
defuit.
sentences.l: and, the other parts having been found, at the place which is midway between the collarbone and the top of the arm, one was missing.
sentences.i: and though the rest were found, at the spot halfway between the collarbone and the top of the arm a piece was missing.
sentences.n: 'aliis repertis' is an ablative absolute — 'with the others found' — and its concessive force ('though the rest were found') has to be supplied from the sense, as ablative absolutes constantly require. 'qui locus est …' is a relative clause doing the work of a noun. 'defuit' has no subject expressed at all: you have to wait two lines for 'partis' to arrive and tell you what was missing, and the delay is the effect — Latin will let a verb stand with nothing to fill its subject until the next sentence supplies it. 'iuguli' and 'summi lacerti' are both genitives governed by 'medius', 'in the middle of'.

sentences.t:
Impositum est non comparentis in usum
partis ebur, factoque Pelops fuit integer illo.
sentences.l: Ivory was set on, for the use of the part not appearing, and by that deed Pelops was whole.
sentences.i: Ivory was fitted in to serve for the part that was not to be found, and by that act Pelops was made whole.
sentences.n: 'in usum' with a genitive is 'to serve as, in place of'. 'comparere' is 'to be visible, to turn up', so 'non comparentis partis' is the piece that never came to light. 'facto … illo' is an ablative absolute closing the part, 'that having been done'. 'integer' is the weight-bearing word: it means untouched, entire, uncut — given here to a body that was cut up, and made true again only by a piece that was never his.
